en: The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*:
A Comprehensive Exposition by the Recluse Ouyi Zhixu of Ancient Wu.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the ultimate discourse of all Buddhas. To begin with, Śākyamuni...
Since the Tathāgata truly attained the Way of the Buddha, an inconceivable number of asaṃkhyeya kalpas have already passed;

yet, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he has never ceased, repeatedly manifesting birth and repeatedly manifesting extinction. He causes those who have not yet planted roots of goodness to plant them;
he causes those who have already planted roots of goodness to bring them to maturity; and he causes those who have already matured to attain liberation.

The flavors of all dharmas are subsumed within the four teachings—Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect; the modes of transformation and instruction are subsumed within the four methods—Sudden, Gradual, Esoteric, and Indeterminate.
Now, based on this particular instance of attaining enlightenment through the eight phases and preaching the Dharma for forty-nine years, it is briefly categorized into five periods:
first, while seated at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, he preached the Mahāyāna for sentient beings of great capacity.
The vehicle of the *Dharmaparyāya* is named the "First Flower Adornment" (*Avataṃsaka*) period; in terms of the method of transformation (*nirmāṇa-vidhi*), it is sudden.
It is like the rising sun first illuminating the high mountains, or like milk being produced from a cow. In terms of the dharma of transformation, it is both Perfect (*yuan*) and Distinct (*bie*):

the Perfect is for those of sharp faculties outside the realms, while the Distinct is for those of dull faculties outside the realms. Thus, those with small capacities have no share in this; they neither see nor hear it, and for this reason, they remain unmoved.

Having attained quiescence at the site of enlightenment, he traveled to the Deer Park to preach the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for the five bhikṣus and others, elucidating the principle of arising and ceasing;
he also taught the phenomena of the twelve links of dependent origination and the six perfections, which is termed the second period of the Āgamas.

In terms of the method of transformation, this marks the beginning of the gradual approach—like the sun shining upon a deep valley, or like curd being produced from milk. In terms of the Dharma of transformation, it constitutes the *Piṭaka* (the Storehouse). However...
Within the realm [of the teaching], those of dull faculties are led to transform from the mundane to the sacred;

next, by means of the mutual exchanges and dialogues of great beings such as Vimalakīrti, the partial is criticized, the small is disparaged, and the Great and the Perfect are extolled—this is called the third period, the *Samatā* (Equal) Period.

Within the gradual aspect of the transformative ritual (*vyavahāra*), this is like the time of eating, or like the production of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) from curd (*dadhi*). Within the transformative doctrine (*dharmaparyāya*), it constitutes the fourth [period].

The teachings are divided into those that discuss both the "half" and the "full," where the *piṭaka* of the Half is termed the "Half-Character Teaching" (*ardhākṣara-dharma*) and the *piṭaka* of the Shared, Distinct, and Complete is termed the "Full-Character Teaching" (*pūrṇākṣara-dharma*).
This enables those of sharp faculties to obtain the benefit of the Full, while those of dull faculties obtain the benefit of the Half;

first, those who have already become sages secretly obtain the benefit of the Shared, and subsequently, together with the four great disciples, he turns the wheel of the Dharma, wherein all dharmas are revealed as the Mahāyāna—this is called the fourth stage.

When, within the provisional teachings, one reaches the end of the gradual approach— just as it is at the *yuzhong* hour [mid-morning], or like obtaining clarified butter (*ghṛta*) from fresh butter— then, within the transformative Dharma,

this serves to clarify the Perfect Teaching (*vimalakīrti-sūtra*) by bringing benefit to those with capacities within the realms through the shared *prajñā* of the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching,
while bringing benefit to those with capacities outside the realms through the unshared *prajñā* of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings, for those who have previously attained sainthood.
Having secretly obtained distinct benefits, he subsequently, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, revealed the provisional to manifest the real and opened up the near to reveal the far;

this is called the fifth period, the time of the *Lotus Sūtra*. In terms of the ritual of transformation, it represents the gradual convergence toward the sudden, and is also termed "neither sudden nor gradual.
It is like the sun’s orb at midday, when the great earth is universally illuminated and no shadows remain; it is also like extracting the refined essence (*sarpis*) from matured butter.
The *Amṛta* (Ghee) among all transformative teachings is pure, perfect, and complete; there is not a single person who cannot attain Buddhahood.

Thus, the original intent of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is finally fulfilled herein. All the skillful means employed by the Tathāgata to transform and deliver sentient beings, as well as the grand framework of the net of teachings, are fully revealed and displayed in this sutra. This is why it alone is named "Wondrous. As for the *Nirvāṇa*, it supports...

In the Vinaya discourses, the teachings generally do not go beyond providing skillful means as a secondary application for those of dull faculties in the final age, in order to lead them to the same realization of ultimate truth.
As for the two modes of transformation—the esoteric and the indeterminate—they pervade the preceding four periods;
however, only the *Lotus Sūtra* is exoteric rather than esoteric, and is definitive rather than indeterminate. This scripture was preached at Vulture Peak, and all who were present...
For eight years, the transmission and preservation [of this text] on palm leaves accumulated to the extent of eight *li*; that which flowed into China consists of three translations in total.

Now, the version translated by Kumārajīva comprises seven fascicles and twenty-eight chapters. Since ancient times, commentators have been numerous and their views inconsistent—some being too concise and others too prolix—such that the essential truth could not be grasped.
It was only when the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai first encountered it at Mount Nanyue...
Dharma Master Huisi was at Mount Dasu in Guangzhou when his teacher entrusted him with the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s ritual arena, commanding him to practice the Lotus Samādhi.
As he recited the sutra to the chapter on the Former Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, the passage stating, "This is true diligence;

this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata," he attained a sudden and great awakening. He entered a state of meditative concentration and personally beheld the assembly on Vulture Peak as it remained solemnly present.

However, before he had dispersed [the assembly], he attained the *ekadharaṇī*. From that time forward, his illumination of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was like the sun and moon shining upon the myriad phenomena;
his penetration of all dharmas was like a pure breeze wandering through the great void. He subsequently explained the general title using the fivefold profound meaning (*pañcavidha-gambhīrārtha*).

Venerable Zhiyi’s disciple, Zhiyan (Zhang’an), recorded these as the ten fascicles of the *Xuan-yi* (Profound Meaning). Furthermore, he analyzed the text according to the four intentions (*catvāraḥ saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).

The *Shìjīngwénzhāng Ān Zūnzhě Jìchéng Wénjù* (Ancestor An’s Record of the Accomplished Textual Commentary on the Explanation of the Sutra) in ten fascicles speaks of the "Fivefold Profound Meaning" (*wǔchóng xuányì*):

first, the title consisting of dharma and metaphor; second, the true reality (*shíxiàng*) as the essence (*tǐ*); third, the One Vehicle’s cause and fruit as the thesis (*zōng*); fourth, the severing of doubt and the engendering of faith as the function (*yòng*);

and fifth, the unsurpassed *amṛta* (clarified butter) as the characteristic of the teaching (*jiàoxiàng*). It further speaks of the "Four Intentions for Interpreting the Text" (*sìyì xiāowén*), the first of which is the cause...

There are four aspects: second, the conditions; third, the teaching; fourth, the original and the trace; and fifth, the contemplation of the mind. The commentary on the text is so vast that I have not had the leisure to provide it in full detail.
Now, I shall briefly set forth the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*). First, regarding the title consisting of the dharma and the metaphor:

the two characters "Wondrous Dharma" (*saddharma*) refer to the dharma, while the two characters "Lotus Flower" (*padma*) refer to the metaphor. To speak briefly of the dharma: there are the dharmas of sentient beings, the dharmas of the Buddha, and the dharmas of the mind.
Furthermore, regarding "wondrousness," to speak briefly, there is the wondrousness of mutual dependence and the wondrousness of non-dependence. As the Sūtra says:

"In order to cause sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (buddhajñānadarśana). If sentient beings lacked the Buddha's knowledge and vision, what would there be to open?

One should know that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are latent within sentient beings; therefore, the phenomena of sentient beings are wondrous. The Buddha-dharma does not transcend the provisional.

The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states: "This Dharma is exceedingly profound and subtle, difficult to see and difficult to fully comprehend; among all classes of sentient beings, none are able to know the Buddha.
This praises the excellence of the ultimate wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*). It further states: "And regarding the other dharmas of the Buddha as well, none are able to fathom them.
This praises the excellence of the provisional wisdom (*upāyajñāna*). Only a Buddha and a Buddha can thoroughly exhaust the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

The Dharma is the provisional that is identical to the real; the true aspect is the real that is identical to the provisional. Therefore, the Buddha-dharma is wondrous. The "Chapter on Peaceful Practices" states:

"Cultivate and restrain the mind to contemplate all dharmas without wavering or retreating. The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sukhāvatī-vyūha* states: "My own mind is inherently empty; sin and merit have no master.
Contemplating the mind as mindless, one realizes that dharmas do not abide. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Contemplate the body..."
The contemplation of the Buddha through the true mark (*dharmatā*) is likewise: the liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings.
As the *Avataṃsaka* states, "Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. Therefore, the dharma of mind is wondrous. Regarding the wondrousness of relativity:

taking the "half-letters" (*ardhamātrā*) as coarse, one clarifies the "full letters" (*pūrṇamātrā*) as wondrous. The Tripiṭaka belongs only to the gate of birth and cessation (the half-letters) and cannot [reveal this].

Because it penetrates and fulfills the principle, the coarse "fulfilling word" (*pūrṇākṣara*) is the gate of non-arising and non-ceasing; because it can penetrate and fulfill the principle, it is subtle.

Furthermore, because the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sutras involve skillful means while penetrating and fulfilling the principle, they are coarse; whereas this present sutra directly reveals the fulfillment of the principle, it is subtle.

Regarding the "subtlety through transcendence," it refers to the teaching of the dharma of non-discrimination: it is the center right at the extremes, wherein there is nothing that is not Buddha-dharma, and all things are extinguished and purified.
In purity, there is no longer any dharma with which to form comparisons; in relation to whom could anything be called coarse and in relation to whom could anything be called subtle?
There is nothing to rely upon and nothing to abandon. Not knowing what name to give it, we forcibly call it "supreme subtlety.
This name is inconceivable; it is not because of coarseness that something is named subtle. If one were to say that only the *dharmadhātu* is vast and uniquely supreme, this would then...
Regarding that which possesses great existence, what is meant by "extinction"? Now, the pure Dharma-realm cannot be shown through waiting, nor can it be shown through extinction;
because it extinguishes waiting and extinguishes extinction, it is called "quiescent extinction" (*śānta-nirvāṇa*).

By means of these two subtleties, the three aforementioned dharmas—the dharmas of sentient beings—also possess these two subtleties, and the dharmas of the Buddha and the dharmas of the mind likewise possess these two subtleties; therefore, they are called the "Subtle Dharma" (*Sūkṣmadharma*). Furthermore...

The detailed explanation of the "Marvelous" (*miao*) consists of the ten marvels of the Trace Gate (*jimen*), the ten marvels of the Origin Gate (*benmen*), and the ten marvels of the Contemplation of the Mind (*guanxin*).

Regarding the ten marvels of the Trace Gate: first, the marvel of the object (*jing*); second, the marvel of wisdom (*zhi*); third, the marvel of practice (*xing*); fourth, the marvel of stages (*wei*); fifth, the marvel of the three dharmas (*sanfa*);

sixth, the marvel of response and resonance (*yinggan*); seventh, the marvel of supernormal powers (*shentong*); eighth, the marvel of preaching the Dharma (*shuofa*); ninth, the marvel of retinues (*juanshu*); and tenth, the marvel of merit and benefit (*gongde lili*).
The realm of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is not created by Buddhas, devas, or humans; it exists inherently from the beginning and is not something that has merely come into being now.

Therefore, at the very outset, because one is deluded regarding the principle, afflictions arise; because one understands the principle, wisdom is born. Wisdom is the foundation of practice: based on the eye of wisdom, the feet of practice are set forth.
These three factors—the eye, the feet, and the objective realm—constitute the vehicle (*yāna*). By means of this vehicle, one enters the Cool Lake (*śītalahrada*).
Ascending to the various stages, in what do they abide? They abide within the secret treasury of the three dharmas. Abiding in these dharmas, they are tranquil yet constantly illuminating;

they respond inevitably to the capacities of beings across the ten realms. When responding to those capacities, they first employ the wheel of the body, using supernatural powers to startle and move them;
next, they employ the wheel of speech to proclaim and guide them. Once they have received the rain of Dharma and accepted the teachings, [they attain realization].
The first five [perfections] fulfill the causes and fruits of one’s own practice;
the latter five fulfill the capacity for transformation and its objects. As the Sūtra says:

"Only Buddhas and Buddhas can thoroughly exhaust the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena," which refers to the fact that all phenomena possess such characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), such natures (*svabhāva*), and so forth.

That this essence is thus, its power is thus, its activity is thus, its causes are thus, its conditions are thus, its fruits are thus, its retributions are thus, and its beginning and end are ultimately equal—this is the excellence of the object (*viṣaya*).

That the wisdom I have attained is subtle, wondrous, and supreme, and that by means of this wondrous wisdom I seek the Unsurpassed Way—this is the excellence of wisdom (*jñāna*). Originally, from countless Buddhas, it has been fully perfected.

Practicing all paths and having completed these paths, one attains the fruit of Buddhahood at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Once the Son of the Buddha has practiced the path, he shall become a Buddha in a future age;

this is precisely the practice of the wondrous. The rain of the four flowers symbolizes the stages of abiding, practice, direction, and realization, as well as the meanings of opening, showing, awakening, and entering—these are the stages.
Riding this precious vehicle, one travels through the four directions straight to the site of enlightenment; the "four directions" represent the causes.
"Abiding in the site of enlightenment" refers to the perfection of the fruit-stage. The Buddha himself dwells in the Great Vehicle;
according to that which he has attained, it is adorned by the power of *samādhi* (concentration) and *prajñā* (wisdom). The Great Vehicle is the track of true nature (*dharmatā-yāna*);

*samādhi* is the track of supportive accomplishment (*pariniṣpatti-yāna*), and *prajñā* is the track of contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā-yāna*). These three factors are the perfection of the Dharma. During the twenty-one days, he contemplated these matters with his Buddha-eye.
The observation and perception of the sentient beings of the six realms is the wondrousness of responsive resonance (*prātihārya*);
entering meditative concentration to cause flowers to rain down, the earth to tremble, and light to be emitted is the wondrousness of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*);

that all the teachings he expounds reach the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), which is now being described as most difficult to believe and difficult to understand, is the wondrousness of the teaching (*deśanā*); it is solely for the purpose of instructing and transforming bodhisattvas.

The śrāvaka disciples are my excellent retinue. Whether in the present or the future, if they hear even a single phrase or a single verse, I shall bestow upon them all the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Upon hearing it for even a moment, they shall immediately attain ultimate *samyak-saṃbodhi*;
I shall not allow even a single person to attain parinirvāṇa alone, but shall cause them all to attain parinirvāṇa through the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
To deliver them is itself the wondrousness of merit and benefit. Regarding the Ten Wondrousnesses of the Fundamental Gate: first, the wondrousness of the fundamental cause;

second, the wondrousness of the fundamental fruit; third, the wondrousness of the fundamental land; fourth, the wondrousness of the fundamental response and resonance; fifth, the wondrousness of the fundamental supernormal powers; sixth, the wondrousness of the fundamental preaching of the Dharma;

seventh, the wondrousness of the fundamental retinue; eighth, the wondrousness of the fundamental nirvana; ninth, the wondrousness of the fundamental lifespan; tenth, the wondrousness of the fundamental benefit.
Regarding "the excellence of the original cause" (*benyin miao*): this refers to the causes cultivated when first generating the bodhicitta and practicing the path of a bodhisattva.

For example, when the sixteen princes propagated the sutra and established karmic connections during the time of Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, these were all deeds performed during the intermediate period and were not the original cause.
The practices undertaken prior to kalpas as numerous as motes of dust are called the excellence of the original cause; this is the original fruit.
"Exquisite" (miao) refers to the original cause—the perfect and exquisite practice from the beginning—which accords with and attains the ultimate permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
this is the "original fruit" (ben guo). It does not mean taking Śākyamuni’s attainment of Buddhahood at the site of tranquility (Ji-chang) as the original fruit;

rather, it takes the fruit first realized since his attainment of Buddhahood, which has been for an exceedingly long time, and names that the "original fruit. Regarding the "exquisite original land," once the original [fruit] is accomplished, it is called "exquisite."

The fruit must necessarily have a basis. Now that his traces are currently in the *sahā* world, or perhaps in the intermediate space between the three lands, there are likewise four lands for the original Buddha;

where, then, does he reside? According to the text, which states: "From that time until now, I have constantly been here in this *Saha* world, preaching the Dharma and teaching and transforming beings," if one follows this passage, it is certainly not the *Saha* world within the present traces.
The "Original" (Ben) is also not a provisional trace or intermediate location; rather, it is the original *Sahā* world, which is precisely the wondrousness of the native land.

As for the "Original Responsive-Induction" (Ben Gan Ying): since the fruit has already been realized, there exists the time of the original realization—the twenty-five sovereign samādhis and the compassionate vows.

Because the capacity and the stimulus are mutually related, one can manifest illumination while remaining in quiescence; therefore, it is called "original responsive-induction. This is the "Original."

As for "supernatural powers," these refer to the neutral transformative meditations (*nirmita-dhyāna*) attained in the past, which, when combined with the various acts of compassion from the time of the original cause, perform transformations that startle and move those sentient beings ready for deliverance; therefore, they are called "original supernatural powers.

As for "original preaching of the Dharma," this refers to the very first turning of the wheel of Dharma immediately upon attaining perfect enlightenment while newly seated at the site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) in the past.
The Dharma spoken through the four analytical knowledges is called the "original teaching.

As for the "original retinue," these are the persons who were the objects of the original teaching, such as those dwelling in the region below whom Maitreya does not recognize; they are the original retinue.
The "original nirvana" refers to the nirvana of the merit of cessation realized at the original time; this is also the provisional means of the shared residence appropriate for that original time.
When the conditions for the two lands have been exhausted, he proclaims his entry into extinction; this is precisely his original *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding his "original lifespan," since he proclaims his entry into extinction, there is a distinction between long and short, or distant and near lifespans. Regarding his "original benefit," this refers to the various merits obtained by his retinue during his original time.
As for the "ten subtleties of contemplating the mind," both the Trace Gate (*jimon*) and the Origin Gate (*honmon*) discuss the trace of contemplating the mind.

The Gate of Contemplating the Mind is scattered throughout various texts. Regarding the gate of contemplating the mind: the Buddha’s suchness and the sentient beings’ suchness are one suchness, an undifferentiated suchness.
Since the Buddha has already contemplated the mind and attained this fundamental wondrous trace, its function is vast and beyond description.
I, as a Tathāgata, and the Buddha’s suchness should likewise contemplate the mind to produce this great benefit; may I, as a Tathāgata, swiftly become like the Buddha’s suchness.
The text says: "If one hears that the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable and, with a profound mind, believes it for even a moment, their merit shall surpass that [of the former].
I vow that in the future I shall have a long life to deliver sentient beings, just as the World-Honored One, the King among the Śākyas, now does;
that I shall roar the lion’s roar at the site of enlightenment and preach the Dharma without fear; and that we, in the future, shall sit upon the path, revered by all."

The teaching regarding lifespan at that time is also like this; this is precisely the sign of obtaining the six stages of identity with the fundamental wondrousness by contemplating the mind, which brings about benefit.
Next, the lotus is explained as a metaphor for the Wondrous Dharma. There are many kinds of flowers; some are "wild flowers" that have no fruit.
The metaphor of one flower yielding many fruits may illustrate how ordinary persons, through their offerings to their parents, receive retribution in the Brahma Heaven;
or, the metaphor of many flowers yielding one fruit may illustrate how Śrāvakas, through various ascetic practices, attain only Nirvāṇa;
or, the metaphor of one flower yielding one fruit may illustrate how Pratyekabuddhas likewise attain [their goal] through a single practice of seclusion.
Nirvāṇa may be compared to the fruit preceding the flower, which can be likened to the Srotāpanna who subsequently practices the Path;

or it may be compared to the flower preceding the fruit, which can be likened to the Bodhisattva who first relies on conditioned cultivation to give rise to subsequent true cultivation. These are all coarse flowers and cannot serve as metaphors for the Subtle Dharma.
Only this lotus flower, with its abundance of both flowers and fruit, can be used as an analogy: the cause contains the myriad practices, and the fruit is the perfection of the myriad virtues.

Furthermore, because the virtue is for the sake of the lotus, the flower and fruit are fully present; this can be used as a metaphor for the identity of the provisional and the real (*jishi er quan*).

The blossoming of the flower and the appearance of the lotus can be used as a metaphor for the identity of the provisional and the real (*jiquan er shi*). The falling of the flower and the completion of the lotus—wherein the lotus is formed and yet the flower falls away—can be used as a metaphor for that which is neither provisional nor real (*feiquan feishi*).

Therefore, the lotus flower is used as a metaphor for the Wondrous Dharma (*miaofa*). Moreover, using this flower as a metaphor, there are three aspects each for the two gates of the Trace and the Origin.

The three aspects of the Parable of the Trace Gate are as follows: First, when a flower blooms, there must necessarily be a lotus; it is for the sake of the lotus that the flower exists, yet the lotus cannot be seen.
This illustrates the intention of establishing the provisional based on the real (*satya*), wherein the real is the ultimate goal, but no one is able to know it.

Second, when the flower opens and the lotus appears, the flower must be used to nourish the lotus. This illustrates that within the provisional there is the real; formerly no one knew this, but now the provisional is opened to reveal the real (*satyaprakāśana*).

The necessity of relying on skillful means to extensively recognize the Buddha-dharma as vast as the sands of the Ganges is solely for the purpose of establishing the Real (the *satya*) so that one may deeply understand the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The three flowers falling and the lotus forming is a parable for the abandonment of the provisional and the establishment of the Real—the Single Buddha Vehicle leading directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Bodhisattvas who possess practice see [this] but not clearly, like the opening of the flowers; because the Buddhas do not engage in practice, they see it [directly].

It is clearly understood, for example, that when the petals fall, the lotus is formed. Regarding the three aspects of the Original Gate (*honmon*): first, just as there must be a lotus within each flower, so too must there be an original basis (*hon*) for every trace (*jaku*).
Although the trace contains the meaning of the original, even though it is the original, the Buddha’s intent is difficult to know; thus Maitreya did not recognize it.

Second, just as the flower opens and the lotus appears, this illustrates the opening of the trace to reveal the original. The intent lies in the fact that through the trace, one can cause the bodhisattvas to recognize the Buddha. Only then...

Once the traces have been recognized, one returns to recognize the fundamental; this is the stage where the path increases and birth is diminished, where the three petals fall and the lotus is perfected.

This serves as an analogy for abandoning the traces to reveal the fundamental. Having recognized the fundamental, one no longer becomes confused by the traces; rather, one cultivates the path within the *dharmakāya* until it reaches perfection on the higher stages.
Furthermore, there are seven metaphors throughout the sutras, all of which illustrate the provisional and the real; here, the lotus flower is used as a comprehensive metaphor for both.
Regarding these seven parables: first, within the Parable of the Burning House, the three carts represent the provisional, while the great white ox-cart represents the real;

second, within the Chapter on Resolving Faith, the parable of the impoverished son uses the employment for wages to represent the provisional and the entrustment of the business to represent the real;

third, the Parable of the Medicinal Herbs uses the three types of grasses and two types of trees to represent the provisional and the single ground to represent the real; fourth, the Parable of the City of Illusion...

The analogy of the conjured city illustrates the provisional; the analogy of the treasure house illustrates the real. In the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions," the parable of the tied jewel illustrates the provisional;
the exchange for a precious jewel illustrates the real. In the "Chapter on the Practice of Peaceful Bliss," the analogy of the wheel-turning king illustrates the provisional;
the untying of the bright jewel from his topknot illustrates the real. These six are all metaphors from the Trace Gate for opening up the provisional and revealing the real.

Furthermore, in the seventh chapter on the Lifespan, the parable of the skilled physician illustrates the provisional through the father’s feigned death and the realization of the truth through his return;
this is precisely the parable from the "Original Gate" that reveals the distant by opening the near.

As for the subsequent two parables of the royal banquet and the well-digging, since they do not fully illustrate the revelation of the One Period, Master Zhiyi omitted them and did not cite them in later generations.
To say that the nine similes [of the Lotus Sūtra] are merely based on the literal text and not its underlying meaning is to rely on the letter rather than the spirit.
"Sūtra" is the general name for the teachings spoken by the Buddha. In Sanskrit, it is called *saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra*.
*Saddharma* translates as "Sublime Dharma" (*miaofa*), and *puṇḍarīka* translates as "Lotus" (*lianhua*). These terms are explained in detail as previously stated.

Because its name differs from other scriptural sources, it is called "distinctive. Since all the teachings given during the course of a single lifetime are termed *sūtra*, it is called "universal *sūtra*.
It may be translated as "discourse" (*jing*), or "agreement" (*qie*), or "basis of the Dharma" (*faben*), or "thread" (*xian*), or "well-spoken instruction" (*shanyu jiao*).
Alternatively, it is said that there is no direct equivalent, yet it encompasses five meanings, the first being "basis of the Dharma."
It is also called "giving birth" (2), "emerging" (3), "displaying" (4), "fountain-heads" (5), "measuring lines" (6), and "stringing garlands" (7).

Translated according to these five categories, they comprise the five *piṭakas*. Each of these five possesses the three aspects of teaching (*śāsana*), practice (*caryā*), and principle (*tattva*). The teaching corresponds to the *loka-vyavahāra-siddhānta*;
practice corresponds to the two types of *pudgala-pratipakṣa-siddhānta*; and principle corresponds to the *paramārtha-siddhānta*. Furthermore, regarding the sages of this land...
To speak of "sūtra" and "sūtra": "dharma" (the teaching) signifies the law and the eternal law; its meaning is that which serves as a standard for guidance.

Because the teaching can be followed, the practice can be followed, and the principle can be followed, it is called "dharma. "Eternal" signifies non-alteration; it cannot be changed or destroyed by celestial Māras or external paths, thus it is the eternity of the teaching.
Being truly authentic and unmixed, with nothing able to surpass it, it is the eternity of practice. It is profoundly still and immovable.
There is absolutely no other destination; this is the constancy of principle. Regarding the two [aspects] having the true mark (*dharmatā*) as their essence:

The Buddha himself speaks of the merit and blessings of propagating the sutra, commanding its circulation; in the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa," the Many-Treasured Buddha and his manifested bodies both bear witness to and assist in this, exhorting others to seek its propagation.
Now, in the tenth chapter, the "Chapter on the Dharma Master": "Dharma" refers to the rules and principles, and a "Master" (śāstṛ) is a teacher and craftsman; though the Dharma may serve as a rule...
The essence [of the Dharma] does not manifest itself; it depends on people for its propagation. Those who have mastered the five kinds of scriptural exegesis may all be called "Masters.

Because they uphold the Dharma to perfect their own practice, taking the wondrous Dharma as their teacher and attaining mastery in their own conduct through that wondrous Dharma, they are called "Dharma-Masters" (*dharmabhāṇaka*).
Furthermore, because they instruct and mold others with the wondrous Dharma, the term "Dharma-Master" is used to designate such a teacher. In this passage, first—
He praised the five kinds of Dharma-preachers who are able to uphold the Dharma: first, receiving and upholding it; second, reading it; third, reciting it;
fourth, explaining it; and fifth, copying it. He subsequently praised the Dharma they uphold and demonstrated the method for penetrating the sūtras, namely:
entering the Tathāgata’s chamber, donning the Tathāgata’s robe, and sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat. The Tathāgata’s chamber is great compassion; if one approaches it according to its nature...
The essence is the Dharmakāya. When it is manifested for sentient beings, it is liberation (*vimukti*); when it enables sentient beings to realize their identity with that same essence, it is Prajñā.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s robe: if considered in terms of what it covers, it is the Dharmakāya; if considered in terms of its ability to adorn the body, it is the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*);
if considered in terms of harmonizing with the light to benefit all things, it is liberation. Thus it is said of the Tathāgata.
As for the "seat": if one considers that which sits upon it, it is Prajñā; if one considers that which is sat upon, it is the Dharmakāya.

When the body and the seat are in profound resonance, it is Liberation. Although they are each distinct, they constitute only a single triad; yet even this triad is not three, so how could they be divided into nine?
Thus, because the Bodhisattva constantly contemplates Nirvāṇa, he exhorts those who propagate the Sūtra to likewise contemplate it constantly.
By contemplating the mind capable of propagating [the Dharma], one understands the principles to be propagated; therefore, the Buddha has you enter my room, don my robes, and sit upon my seat.
If these three dharmas were absent, what would it mean to propagate the sutras?
The eleventh chapter, "Seeing the Jeweled Stupa," describes how the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna emerges from the earth and is seen by the entire assembly, who then hear a great voice;
this serves to authenticate the previous gathering of Buddhas and to introduce the subsequent opening of the stupa.
The twelfth chapter, "Devadatta," [explains that] Devadatta means "Heavenly Heat. When he was born, humans and devas experienced a feverish heat;
for this reason, he was given this name. His conduct was contrary to the Way, and he was originally a teacher of the Buddha.

Because sentient beings are scorched by the heat of afflictions (*kleśa*), the Bodhisattva manifested the appearance of sharing in their illness to deliver them. Within the text, it first clarifies Devadatta’s past life.

In the previous section on the Sutra-transmission, it was clearly explained how Śākyamuni attained enlightenment; today, it is explained how Mañjuśrī transmits the sutra and the dragon girl attains Buddhahood.
The thirteenth chapter, the "Chapter on Upholding," contains both the practice of upholding and the exhortation to uphold.

The fourteenth chapter, "The Practice of Peaceful Conduct" (*Anrakugyō-bon*), is explained according to its objective basis as follows: because the body is free from danger, it is peaceful; because the mind is free from anxiety and affliction, it is blissful;
and because both body and mind are peaceful and blissful, one is able to advance in practice. By donning the robe of the Tathāgata, the Dharma-body is established;
by entering the hall of the Tathāgata, the mind of liberation is joyful; and by sitting upon the seat of the Tathāgata, one proceeds with wisdom as the guide.
This is the commentary on the text of the "Superior Chapter" (*uttama-paṭala*). Because he dwells on the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), his body is at ease and not impetuous;

because his mind joyfully contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, he advances. This is the commentary on the text of the "Chapter on Advancing" (*pratipatti-paṭala*). "Peaceful" (*śānta*) means immovable;

it cannot be moved by the six realms of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) or by the two types of noble ones (*ārya*) in nirvāṇa. "Bliss" (*sukha*) means the samādhi of non-reception and non-non-reception (*anupādānānupādāna-samādhi*).
The vast function does not admit the five feelings of ordinary beings, nor even the five feelings arising from views within the Perfect Teaching;

these too are all not admitted. Where there is feeling, there is suffering; where there is no feeling, there is no suffering. Being without suffering and without pleasure is called the practice of Great Bliss, the practice of non-practice, and the practice of neither practicing nor not practicing.
It is called "non-practice" because one neither practices the ways of ordinary beings nor practices the ways of sages and saints. Thus it is termed "non-practice."

To practice the Middle Way is therefore called "practicing this Dharma-gate. This commentary consists of four sections, which involve guiding the three karmas through *śamatha* (calm abiding), *vipaśyanā* (insight), compassion, and the vow.
Regarding the bodily karma: because there is *śamatha*, one leaves behind coarse physical actions;
because there is *vipaśyanā*, one does not apprehend a body, nor does one apprehend bodily karma. Because one does not apprehend that which could be left behind, there is non-apprehension.
Because they possess compassion, they do not fall into the state of ordinary worldlings, but diligently cultivate their physical actions to extensively benefit all beings.

Because they possess the practice of *śamatha*, they do not fall into the stages of the two vehicles (*hīnayāna*). Wearing the robe of patience because they possess the practice of *vipaśyanā*, they sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat.

Because they possess compassion, they enter the Tathāgata’s chamber. Through the practice of *śamatha* being free from faults, they realize the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*); through the practice of *vipaśyanā* being non-attached, they realize wisdom (*jñāna*).
Virtue consists of compassion and benefiting others, which constitutes "beneficence"; beneficence supports and perfects "wisdom-virtue," and wisdom-virtue is able to penetrate "abandonment-virtue.

This is called the "peaceful conduct of bodily action"; the same applies to the vows of speech and mind. Up to this point, the section on the Trace (the provisional teaching) for the circulation [of the Dharma] is concluded.
The fifteenth chapter, "The Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth," concerns the Great Beings of the Dharma-body who dwell in the space below;
these were originally disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha, and having now received his command, they have emerged to propagate this sutra.
Even Maitreya does not recognize them, and it is from this that the great teaching which reveals the distant by opening up the near is initiated.
Chapter Sixteen: The Lifespan of the Tathāgata. This chapter correctly reveals the immediate traces while manifesting the distant origin.

"Tathāgata" is a general designation for all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods—whether two Buddhas, three Buddhas, the Original Buddha, or the Trace-Buddha. "Lifespan" (*āyuṣ*) means that which is received;
"measure" (*pramāṇa*) means to evaluate or define. Here, the text precisely defines the merits of the Reward Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) of the original ground, and the wisdom of that Reward Body.

Because the upper [realm] is harmonized with the profound and the lower [realm] accords with it, such that the three bodies (*trikāya*) are perfectly complete, it is called the "Chapter on the Life Span of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the seventeenth chapter, the "Chapter on the Differentiation of Merits": because the Buddha has taught the life span and his disciples throughout the three periods of time have obtained various benefits, it is called "merit";
because these merits vary in depth and shallowness, it is called "differentiation. Within this chapter, there is the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) and the acceptance thereof.
The explanation of the *Circulation* (Pravartana) section: the Buddha’s discourse on the long prose is the general bestowal of the prediction of the Dharmakāya;

Maitreya’s verses are the general exposition of the understanding and acceptance of this. What follows constitutes the *Circulation* section. Within it, first the four kinds of faith in the present life are clarified, followed by the five grades after extinction.

Regarding the four kinds of faith: first, faith and understanding in every thought-moment, though not yet capable of expounding the teaching; second, a brief understanding of the verbal expressions; third, [the subsequent grades].
Extensively explaining this to others constitutes the fifth stage, the accomplishment of the five grades of practitioners: first, the arising of a mind of sympathetic joy;
second, adding one's own upholding, receiving, and reciting; third, adding the exhortation of others to uphold, receive, and recite; fourth, adding the concurrent practice of the six perfections;
and fifth, adding the correct practice of the six perfections.
Chapter Eighteen: The Merit of Rejoicing. This chapter clarifies the causal merit of the initial stage to encourage the circulation [of this teaching].
"Following" (*anuparivarta*) means to accord with principle and phenomena as being non-dual and undifferentiated. "Rejoicing" (*muditā*) refers to celebrating both oneself and others.

To accord with principle means that upon hearing of the Buddha’s profound and remote original ground, one believes and accords with it deeply, without opposition, and without even a hair’s breadth of doubt or stagnation. To accord with phenomena means that upon hearing of the Buddha’s three... [the text continues].
Benefiting the world and all beings, it pervades horizontally and vertically throughout all places without a single hair’s breadth of doubt or obstruction.

It possesses the merit of reality that accords with principle, the merit of expedient means that accords with phenomena, and the wisdom that rejoices in oneself and the compassion that rejoices in others.
Because these—expedient means and reality, wisdom and severance—are explained in combination, it is called the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing."

The nineteenth chapter, "The Merits of the Dharma Master," clarifies the merits of the fruit of the initial stage to encourage the circulation [of the teaching], namely, the purification of the six sense faculties. The twentieth chapter,

"The Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging," cites the retribution for faith and slander, as well as merit and demerit, to provide further proof and encouragement for the circulation [of the teaching] while harboring [the truth] within.
Because he did not slight others, his understanding was beyond external respect; because he did not slight others, his physical presence established the practice of non-slighting;
because he did not slight others, his speech proclaimed the teaching of non-slighting; and because people called him by the name "Never-Disparaging," he was named *Sadāparibhūta*.

The above three chapters and a half conclude the section on exhorting the upholding and circulation [of the sutra]. What follows in the next eight chapters clarifies the entrustment and circulation, which is further divided into:
The three chapters on the "Entrustment through Spiritual Power" (Shenli Zhulèi) clarify the entrustment and circulation [of the teaching].

The five chapters beginning with "Medicine King" (Yaowang) encourage circulation by means of transforming others, while the single chapter on "Samantabhadra" (Puxian) encourages circulation by means of one's own practice.

The twenty-first chapter, "The Supernatural Powers of the Tathāgata" (*Tathāgata-ṛddhi-bala-parivarta*): "Supernatural" (*ṛddhi*) refers to the unfathomable, and "power" (*bala*) refers to efficacious function.

Because the unfathomable signifies the profoundness of the natural body (*dharmakāya*), and efficacious function signifies the greatness of the power of transformation, this chapter is named "The Chapter on Supernatural Powers" because it manifests ten kinds of great powers in order to entrust the profound Dharma.
The twenty-second chapter, "Entrusting" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*): "Entrusting" (*pari*) refers to that which the Buddha has entrusted;

"cumulative" (*nanda*) refers to your diligent proclamation of this [teaching]. This name is derived from the holy intent. Furthermore, "entrusting" refers to receiving the entrustment upon the crown of one's head;

"cumulative" refers to doing so with joy rather than weariness. This name is derived from the Bodhisattva’s respectful compliance. Moreover, "entrusting" refers to what is entrusted by the golden mouth of the Tathāgata; "cumulative" refers to the Bodhisattva.

With a loyal heart, I receive this as it was transmitted from teacher to disciple; therefore, the Tathāgata rose from his seat in person, extended his hand to stroke my head, and bestowed upon me this dharma that is difficult to encounter.
The great assembly bowed their bodies and joined their palms, saying, "We shall faithfully carry out what the World-Honored One has commanded.
Because this was a solemn transmission of the teaching, it is called *parindanā* (entrustment).

The twenty-third chapter, "The Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja," exhorts masters who propagate the Dharma that they should exhaust their spiritual powers and the full span of their lives to spread the Great Dharma.

The twenty-fourth chapter, "The Sublime Sound," and the twenty-fifth chapter, "The Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara," both exhort the disciples who receive the Dharma to know that the Great Beings of other lands have received their mandate to propagate this sutra. They universally manifest forms in accordance with the physical appearances [of beings], yet these forms have no fixed standard;
they cannot be viewed with the eyes of cattle or sheep, nor can they be fathomed by the ordinary consciousness of commoners. Regarding what has been heard here, do not—
If one gives rise to thoughts of contempt, such thoughts will not defile the mind with regard to the Dharma.
As for the twenty-sixth chapter, "Dhāraṇī," because the propagation of the sutras in the degenerate age is frequently beset by afflictions and obstacles,
these dhāraṇīs are used to protect them so that the Way may flow forth.
The twenty-seventh chapter, "The Past Deeds of King Subhavyūha," explains the prior conditions of the four noble ones to manifest the merit of protecting human beings.
The twenty-eighth chapter, "The Exhortation of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva"— the Sanskrit term *Samantabhadra* is translated as [普賢]— is as follows:
Samantabhadra is also translated as "Universal Auspiciousness" (*Pianji*); his name is "Universal" (*Pu*) because it pervades all paths, and "Worthy" (*Xian*) because it reaches the ultimate limit.

His exhortation is an expression of devotion to the Dharma. Having heard the beginning and end of this sutra in its entirety while remaining in that distant land, and desiring to ensure that his own practice and his transformation of others continue forever without end, he has come from the east to offer this exhortation.
Furthermore, regarding the sequence of the arising of the eleven chapters and a half of the *Pravartana* (Circulation) section:

as stated above, those who hear the sutra in the present age obtain both the true and the semblance benefits. However, even if one merely hears a single phrase and gives rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), its merit is comparable to that of the "Fourfold Faith" of the present;
lest people should doubt that such merit is small because no Buddha will appear in the future, [the text] speaks of the five [aspects] after the extinction [of the Buddha].
The merits of the stage [of practice] are subtle and hidden, not as manifest as the merits of the fruit; therefore, the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" is taught.

Cause and effect are presented together, yet this is not as clear as providing scriptural citations; therefore, the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging" is taught. Although past individuals are cited, this is not as effective as demonstrating present transformations;

therefore, the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" is taught. Although supernatural powers are displayed, this is not as significant as the bestowing of the seal through the touching of the crown of the head.

Although the discourse on entrustment generally covers all aspects of entrustment, it does not equal showing its essential method: discarding the body to preserve the Way; therefore, it speaks of the Medicine King.

Although it exhorts those who transform others, it does not equal exhorting those who are transformed: wherever one hears the Dharma, one should conceive the thought of a Buddha; therefore, it speaks of Wonderful Sound and Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, if those with initial resolve propagate the sutra yet lack supernatural powers, they must rely on internal prohibitions; therefore—

Because the teaching of the dhāraṇī further requires external protection, the King of Adornment (Samantabhadra) is described as appearing in successive layers to ensure that the Great Dharma is widely propagated.
Furthermore, Samantabhadra again requests the correct exposition to encourage his own practice, and again requests its circulation to encourage the transformation of others.
The Buddha answers with four methods in total: first, being protected and remembered by all Buddhas; second, ... [text continues]
Third, planting the roots of all virtues; fourth, giving rise to the mind that seeks to rescue all sentient beings.

These two points constitute the direct answer and the general purport for the circulation [of this teaching]. Why is this? Although the Buddha is without partiality, if one can distance oneself from evil and follow what is good, turn back from delusion and return to the correct, and understand the provisional teachings while realizing the Buddha’s own knowledge and vision, then one will accord with the Sage’s heart. Thus, [the text] says: "All..."

If the Buddha protects and remembers one, and if the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened, then Prajñā will illuminate; this is the planting of the roots of all virtues, and it is also entry into the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
It is neither distracted, nor savoring, nor grasping, nor abandoning; it is the arousal of the mind to rescue sentient beings.

One should know that these four and the "opening of the provisional to reveal the real" differ in name but are identical in essence—there is no duality and no distinction. Furthermore, it is the Buddha’s protection and remembrance.

"Opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers to planting the roots of all virtues; "showing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers to giving rise to the mind that seeks to save sentient beings;

"awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers to entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*); and "entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers to the essential gateway of the traces.

These four encompass it all. Furthermore, since the traces have their source, and one opens, shows, awakens to, and enters [the truth] by following that source, there is the opening, showing, awakening, and entering within the traces.
To realize and enter [this truth] now, the provisional traces are opened to reveal the fundamental reality; thus, the fundamental and the trace are non-dual and without distinction.
To answer his request with these four dharmas makes the meaning perfectly clear. Regarding the propagation of the teaching by answering his request with these four dharmas:

the methods for propagation are only three or four. To give rise to the mind that rescues sentient beings is to enter the Tathāgata’s chamber. To enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and be protected by the Buddha's mindfulness is...
Donning the robes of the Tathāgata and planting the roots of all virtues is the essential method for proclaiming [the Dharma]; this constitutes three out of the four [anle-hang].
Furthermore, generating the mind to save sentient beings is the vow-based *anle-hang*; entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) is the mental *anle-hang*;
planting the roots of all virtues is the verbal *anle-hang*; and being protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas is the physical *anle-hang*.
One should know that the latter four practices of joyful conduct are identical to the former four. First, in response to his two requests, he cites these four as a comprehensive summary.
Is this not both skillful and wondrous, as the *Lotus Sūtra* is thus re-expounded? May even a single phrase moisten the spirit so that all may be aided toward the further shore;
may reflection and cultivation forever serve as a vessel for crossing over; and may those who rejoice in or witness and hear [this teaching] always act as primary or auxiliary companions.
Whether grasping or relinquishing, may these scriptures pass through my ears to become conditions—whether favorable or adverse—so that I may ultimately be liberated by them.
On the day of my liberation, may the primary and secondary retributions constantly proclaim this wondrous scripture; may not even a single land or a single atom fail to benefit sentient beings.

I pray that all Buddhas will secretly infuse their transformative power and support me, and that all Bodhisattvas will secretly lend their majestic spiritual authority, so that wherever they have not yet been preached, I may everywhere entreat them to do so.

Wherever there is a place of teaching, one should personally receive and make offerings; through a single phrase or a single verse, one advances toward Bodhi, and through a single color or fragrance, one shall never regress.
This is the weaving together of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Postscript:
Formerly, when Li Qinglian (Li Bai) ascended the Yellow Crane Tower and saw the poem inscribed by Cui Hao, he immediately set down his brush, knowing that it could not be surpassed.
When the Great Master Zhi (Zhiyi) personally realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra, even the Guangzhai Temple was already surpassed [by his realization].
It may be known that my descendants have been numerous and active, yet their discerning eyes remain unrefined because they lack the learning of the Blue Lotus.
Having already composed this esoteric treatise on the *Buddhāvatamsaka* (Fo ding), my friends all requested that I further explain the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
I declined based on these considerations, but it so happened that while expounding this wondrous scripture at Ziyun Temple, my dharma friend Dajie urged me to publish the Sanskrit text.

Desiring to summarize the essential purport of the entire sutra for the convenience of beginners, I have respectfully followed the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) and *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) to extract the main outlines, naming this work *Lunguan* (The Threaded Summary).
It is my hope that by merely dipping one’s finger into it, one may come to know the flavor of the entire cauldron.
If others should mock me for transcribing the writings of predecessors, how could I dare refuse? Written with reverence by Ouyi Zhixu.
